catalog_quote: Like most of the Trans-Himalayan languages, Monsang is a tone language. From the data collected, we discovered two tones, which we called them as high tone and low tone; similarly, Konnerth (2018) has also mentioned about the presence of two tones in Monsang. [...] For instance, initially the word in (toneless) ‘curry’ is understood as ‘low tone’ when compared with the word í:n (high tone) ‘house’. However, the word in (toneless) ‘curry’ is a toneless word, and the word í:n (high tone) `house’ is a `high tone’ word because the word í:n (high tone) `house’ contrasts with the word ì:n (low tone) ‘drink’, as they both have long vowels [...] The tone-bearing unit (henceforth TBU) in Monsang is considered as the syllable. [...] The acoustic results show that there are two distinct tones in Monsang: High and Low. Phonetically, the two tones fall slightly at the end of the f0 duration (see figure 24). [...] This preliminary analysis shows that there are pitch contrasts only in limited words. Our next research work on tone will be, ‘How do the ‘toneless’ words surface in prosodic terms and the tone pattern in multi-syllabus or phrases?’

new_statements.rule_in_words: Monsang is described as a lexical tone language with two tones (High, Low) whose tone-bearing unit is the syllable; the only dedicated phonology (and Konnerth 2018, Konnerth & Wanglar 2019, Mortensen 2023) says nothing at all about word stress or accent, and explicitly defers the prosody of 'toneless' words and polysyllables to future work. No statement of stress placement exists in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: Some words are 'toneless' (e.g. in 'curry'); bare verb stems neutralise to low tone (Konnerth 2018: 26 fn; Konnerth & Wanglar 2019: 55); tone patterns on prefixed disyllables inconsistent (Konnerth 2018 sec. 2.5). None of this is framed as stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Tone data are citation forms (isolation token before a carrier phrase), monosyllables; polysyllabic/phrasal prosody explicitly not yet studied. Variety: Monsang Pantha (first author's), cross-checked with two other speakers.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe the same language, Monsang [nmh] = mons1234 (autonym Sirti, sirti ṭoŋ). Monsang & Veikho 2018 is based on the Monsang Pantha village variety (first author native speaker, cross-checked with two others); Konnerth & Wanglar's data come from Liwachangning village. No dialect-level glottocodes exist under mons1234.
